text: Among the merits Johnson assigns to Shakespeare, one is stated with his usual plainness: "Shakespeare has no heroes; his scenes are occupied only by men" (Johnson 1765). The other dramatists, as Johnson saw them, lifted their persons above the common level of mankind; they lent them sentiments which no living man would utter, and a manner of speech contrived to be admired, though it could hardly be believed. Shakespeare declined this practice, and Johnson reckons the refusal among his chief excellences. The persons of the plays speak as the reader himself would have spoken, had he stood in the same place and felt the same pressure. Their words are taken from ordinary life; and they move us because in them we recognise ourselves. This holds even where the action passes beyond probability. A ghost upon the platform, or witches meeting on the heath, lies wholly outside experience; but the speech of those who behold such things remains within it. The marvel is confined to the plot, and the dialogue keeps the level of life. Hamlet questions the spirit of his father as any son might question a thing so dreadful. Macbeth broods upon the prophecy as an ambitious man would brood upon the promise of a crown.
